newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Papal visit seen as political event in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Papal visit seen as political event in Bosnia.

text.p: Pope John Paul's historic visit to the predominantly Moslem city of Sarajevo carries significant political weight in Bosnia after a war that fed on religious differences.
Bosnian Moslem leaders have gone out of their way to welcome the Pope to the capital where Croat Catholics now comprise less than 10 percent of the population.
Sarajevo state television has devoted extensive coverage to preparations for the Papal tour and plans to broadcast his open-air mass on Sunday in Kosevo Olympic stadium.

The Pope's early and outspoken support of Bosnian statehood makes him a sympathetic figure to Moslem leaders. "His visit is a sign of recognition," Alija Izetbegovic, Moslem chairman of the collective presidency, said this week.
Izetbegovic urged his supporters to "do your best to greet him with all the dignity and respect he deserves".
By choosing to visit the capital Sarajevo, instead of the heavily Catholic region of Herzegovina, the Pope had shown his sympathies lie with Croat moderates, political analysts said.

"It's significant because the Pope is clearly backing the moderate Croats by coming to Sarajevo and not coming to the hardline homeland of Herzegovina," said historian Chris Bennett, author of a book on the Yugoslav conflict.

Papal speeches promoting religious tolerance and Bosnian independence will provide a clear counterpoint to the nationalist rhetoric coming from the nationalists in the southwestern Herzegovina region, Bennett told Reuters.
"The Pope is showing them that they can and should actually live together."
The Catholic cardinal of Bosnia, Vinko Puljic, strongly supports the Pope's calls for co-existence among Moslems, Catholic Croats and Orthodox Christian Serbs.
But the 51-year old cardinal wields little influence over the hardline clergy in his church.
Although Bosnia's religious leaders have taken tentative steps towards restoring a dialogue after the 1992-95 conflict, analysts say intolerance is still the rule in Bosnia.
The 25-hour visit by the Pope, however widely publicised, may not be enough to counter the firmly entrenched nationalists who rule over rival ethnic communities, analysts said.
Orthodox Christian Serbs still view the Vatican with hostility because of its early recognition of Croatian and Bosnian independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia.
Pope John Paul tried to visit Sarajevo in September 1994 when the war was raging but had to cancel the trip because Serb forces laying siege to the city refused to offer security guarantees.
The Serb member of the country's new collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, has quietly agreed to this visit.
The Pope meets separately with each member of the three-man presidency on Sunday. His scheduled nine-minute talk with Krajisnik would have been unthinkable only a year ago.
Krajisnik, however, has managed to inject politics into the protocol.

The hardline nationalist has refused to attend arrival and departure ceremonies at Sarajevo airport, citing security concerns. Diplomats said Krajisnik wanted to make clear that he did not share the enthusiasm of other presidency members for the Pope's views.
